vignette: Ten years ago, Julian Vance was sexually assaulted in the cramped, dimly lit corridor behind a Chicago venue while on tour. The night does not register as a timeline; instead, it arrives in fractured shards. Some moments of the encounter are blindingly sharp-the glint of a belt buckle, the slick warmth of blood spreading across his sleeve-while the hours before and after dissolve into a complete void. Unable to tell a clear story of what happened even to himself, he learned early on to push the memory away before he could fully recall it. This constant avoidance did not erase the event; rather, it allowed unresolved fragments to leak into his waking hours, sharpening his sensitivity to environmental cues. Within weeks, the mere scent of a specific cologne or the sight of another man's violent stance would instantly lock his body into survival mode, convincing him that danger was imminent. Julian's nervous system settled into a permanent state of anticipatory threat. He found himself feeling safe only in a highly circumscribed set of rooms in his own home, while the outside world quickly narrowed to perceived hazards. When colleagues or venue staff moved quickly around him, his posture would stiffen immediately, every muscle braced against a sudden motion that might signal another attack. This relentless scanning of the environment disrupted his ability to process the trauma, ensuring that the memory remained blocked before he could ever work through it. The unresolved nature of the memory fed directly into his sense of danger, convincing him that the assault was still actively unfolding in his periphery. His hypervigilance did not just protect him; it actively manufactured the very reminders he feared, causing him to misinterpret neutral gestures or ordinary scents as credible warnings. Living inside this closed loop of dread forced Julian to adopt rigid survival habits. The constant, simmering irritability and sudden flashes of anger that bubbled up inside him were immediately extinguished; he had come to believe that feeling or expressing anger would only make him vulnerable again. Because the trauma memory remained fragmented and refused to settle into a coherent narrative, he felt compelled to construct these rigid behaviors to manage the confusion. He stopped attending industry gatherings, carefully avoiding seeing anyone he had socialized with before the event, and steered clear of being around people in authority or uniform. By never allowing himself to process the fear or anger trapped in his chest, he starved the memory of the emotional processing it needed, keeping it trapped in a state of partial clarity. The rigid avoidance of social contacts and safe zones only ensured that every minor trigger would continue to register as an active, unmitigated alarm. Now, at fifty-six, Julian's career as a session musician has shrunk to match his narrowing world. He accepts only studio work that requires zero travel, yet even the familiar soundproof booth in his neighborhood recording space has become a battleground. Last month, during a tracking session, the audio engineer stepped in wearing that same heavy, cloying cologne and knocked sharply on the glass door. Julian's hands flew to his ears, his breath hitching as the room tilted and his hands shook uncontrollably. He realized he had missed three consecutive days of work and was actively withdrawing from his wife, fearing that his own unpredictable temper would spill onto her. What finally brought him to the clinic was not the nightmares, which were manageable with medication, but the terrifying realization that the music he once loved had become a trigger, and that his only coping strategy was a suffocating silence that was costing him his career and his marriage. He hopes to find a way to separate the past from the present without having to confront the anger he has spent a decade burying.
